doc.title: Abe Most interviewed by Monk Rowe, Los Angeles, California, February 13, 1999

title: Clarinet on Northern Exposure with David Schwartz
summary: He played clarinet for Schwartz's synth-based scores, the doctor character's instrument, and talks about composer cue royalties.

story.theme_name: Jazz musicians in the movies and film scoring
story.community_name: Jazz musicians on film and studio scoring

blocks.x: Tell me about — I have to ask about “Northern Exposure.”

That was a lot of fun. David Schwartz, who was the writer, that was the first time I had — not the first time, I had been with some people who had used synths. Now David is a bass player and used synth for whatever sounds he wanted, and he used that as when he did his work he would work on the synth and then he’d say, “Oh this ought to be a clarinet, and this ought to be a” so and so. And he would play me, when I came in he would play what he wanted on the clarinet sound, he’d say, “Play something like this” but use your own style, use your own thing. So as a matter of fact he let me, on one of these Northern things he said, “Well I need some time so why don’t you start off with a minute of noodling.” So he put my name down. I don’t know if I ever got any money for that but—

No credit, I never got any credit. But that was — it was usually one or two instruments at a time added to what he already had. For instance, if he had a piano, a synth or a drummer would come in and play the actual thing, a lot of times the drummer came later, or a guitarist, or he’d have just three or four people in the whole thing. By the time he got through he had a whole orchestral sound but he didn’t use large orchestras. It was four or five maybe, unless he had I remember a couple of times maybe he had — I don’t know if he had a string quartet ever, he might have a couple of times. But mostly he’d call me and say I need some clarinet stuff for this guy. Usually, the clarinet was the doctor, remember, the main character initially was the Jewish doctor who gave up life in New York to now spend some time out here. So I was that character. So whenever the doctor — I forgot his name, I don’t know why.

Joel, right. So whenever he did something, the clarinet would be playing a little something. So that’s usually, in the old days — the old days, 20 or 30 years back, usually they would assign an instrument to a character. Al Newman, all the big composers would do that. In the big pictures they would have a trumpet above the orchestra signifying a big field with a lot of dead bodies — you know. That would be his theme for that—
The signature for that particular type of scene. But in this case, each character had an instrument that he would use — I’m talking about David — to play that particular

character. So a lot of composers did that sort of thing. But in this case, I used to enjoy that show. They had great actors, actresses — I don’t know if they want to be called actresses — actors. But it was a great show.
Yeah. Very quirky and— Now it’s in syndication. Do you get any—
The composer gets cue time. I mean every time a cue is played the composer gets a credit. For instance like Mike Post, who does — there’s some lawyer picture I forgot, we watch it once in a while.

“L.A. Law,” one of those. [scats] Now every time there’s a chance [scats] I’m sure he makes a fortune — and it gripes me because I could have done [scats] if I had a chance. It doesn’t gripe me that he’s making money, but he is, he’s one of those.
What a racket. Yeah. He’s written quite a few.
Yeah, but David is a bright guy and he does some nice things, David Schwartz I’m talking about, “Northern Exposure.”
